meta.name: WasteWise knowledge base (draft v0.1)
meta.status: DRAFT for team verification. Do not show to end users as-is.
meta.jurisdiction: Lagos State plus federal (NESREA) rules only. Other states are not covered.
meta.method: Compiled from web search results and page excerpts. Claims are paraphrased, not copied. Official LAWMA and NESREA websites could not be crawled directly; NESREA material came via a NESREA-hosted PDF and the FAOLEX legal database, and WHO material via its fact sheet excerpts. World Bank, UNEP and Basel Convention documents were not retrieved.
meta.how_to_read: 'facts' are statements traceable to the listed sources. In 'household_guidance', basis='source' means a source states it; basis='derived' means a team inference from the sources that a human should verify. Empty lists mean nothing reliable was found; they are not an oversight.
meta.date_warning: Several news pages showed a site banner date (for example July or August 2026) that is NOT the article date. Where an article date was not clearly visible it is marked 'not captured'.
meta.no_prices: Buy-back and scrap prices appeared in some sources but are old or undated, so they are deliberately left out.

jurisdiction_notes.note: Lagos household bin rules are inconsistent across sources. A September 2022 announcement described one bin for plastic and one for organic waste from January 2023. A later LAWMA statement (article date not captured) described a general-waste bin and a recyclables bin. Do not hard-code either; show 'check current LAWMA guidance'.
Lagos has said it plans to make sorting waste at source mandatory (reported in 2026). The exact start date and rules were not found.
LAWMA says households must keep bins and subscribe to licensed private sector participation (PSP) collectors, and that residents should contact LAWMA if their PSP operator fails to collect.
LAWMA has urged residents to sort waste at source into recyclables and non-recyclables and use designated bins.

facts.claim: Lagos's single-use plastics ban, enforced from 1 July 2025, does not cover PET bottles or sachet water.
In Lagos and Ogun, PET moves from collectors to recycling plants; one recycler said white PET (water and soda bottles) is what buyers want, and that bottle quality and type matter.
Bottle caps are made of polypropylene, and at least one recycler separates and resells them to a sister company.
LAWMA has run a buy-back programme at designated points that bought clean plastic bottles (undated; prices in the source are old and omitted).
Informal waste pickers in Lagos are paid by weight, which favours rigid plastics such as bottles.

household_guidance.text: Keep PET bottles separate from food and wet waste so they stay clean enough for collectors and recyclers.
Give them to a collector, buy-back point or recycler instead of dumping them.

categories.where_to_take: Not verified. No current consumer drop-off addresses were confirmed. Ask LAWMA or a local recycler.
gaps: Whether caps should stay on or come off

facts.claim: Pure water sachets are exempt from the Lagos single-use plastics ban.
A 2014 review of Lagos flood management listed pure water sachets among the materials that clog drains and contribute to flooding.
Waste pickers paid by weight tend to skip light sachets.
A LAWMA buy-back bought sachets only if clean and moisture-free, and LAWMA recycled them into black nylon bags (undated source).

A 2020 pilot (Project ReflexNG) aimed to divert 600 tonnes of sachets and funded a stationary buy-back centre run by RecyclePoints at the Lagos State Ministry of Environment premises. Whether it still operates was not verified.

household_guidance.text: Keep used sachets clean and dry if you plan to hand them to a buyer.
Do not throw sachets into drains or canals.

categories.where_to_take: Not verified. Check whether the RecyclePoints or LAWMA buy-back points still operate.

facts.claim: Several Lagos recycling companies buy empty aluminium drink cans from scavengers and waste resource merchants; one converts them into sheets for new cans (older, undated article).
A Lagos waste-business owner said iron, paper, plastics, rubber, foams, food waste and glass are also recycled and in demand.
LAWMA's neighbourhood sorting scheme was described as separating metal cans, paper and glass (undated).

household_guidance.text: Aluminium drink cans can be handed to scrap collectors or can-buying recyclers.

categories.where_to_take: Local scrap dealers or can recyclers. Specific current buyers not verified.

facts.claim: A Lagos waste-business owner said glass is recycled and in demand.
LAWMA's neighbourhood sorting scheme was described as treating glass separately (undated).
In 2022 LAWMA's MD said less than 10 percent of recyclables were being collected in Lagos, and AFP reported plastic, metal and glass are mostly thrown away in Nigeria.

gaps: Safe handling of broken glass (no source retrieved)

facts.claim: A Lagos waste-business owner said paper is among the recycled materials in demand.
LAWMA's neighbourhood sorting scheme was described as separating paper (undated).

gaps: How cartons and waxed or laminated packs are treated

facts.claim: LAWMA's MD said about 6,500 of the roughly 13,000 tonnes of waste Lagos produces daily is organic and should be turned into compost or biomethane rather than landfilled.
LAWMA runs a compost plant at Odogunyan, Ikorodu, producing compost fertiliser (undated).
LAWMA says it commissioned a biodigester at the Ikoyi Fruit Market that converts fruit waste to energy (article date not captured).
A 2022 announcement said households should use a separate bin for organic waste; later statements describe different bin splits.

household_guidance.text: Put food waste in the household bin collected by your assigned PSP operator, and check current LAWMA guidance on whether organics need a separate bin.

categories.where_to_take: Household collection by PSP operator. No public drop-off for food waste was found.

facts.claim: NESREA's National Environmental (Battery Control) Regulations, 2024 exist. Their development began in 2020 after public concern over crude handling of used lead-acid batteries.
Producers, importers and distributors of batteries must manage the environmental impact of their products and subscribe to an extended producer responsibility (EPR) programme.
NESREA has registered the Alliance for Responsible Battery Recycling (ARBR) as the producer responsibility organisation for the battery sector.
Organisations using lead-acid batteries for energy storage, vehicle fleets and telecoms are required to inform ARBR for collection. This concerns organisations, not households.
Lead-acid batteries contain corrosive sulphuric acid and large amounts of lead.

Used lead-acid batteries are collected informally by scavengers, retailers and scrap yards; reporting found local recyclers breaking batteries open to extract lead and threatening community health in Lagos and Ogun.
Indiscriminate disposal and recycling of lead-acid and lithium-ion batteries in Nigeria releases lead, lithium, cadmium, nickel and acids.

household_guidance.text: Do not dump batteries or break them open; the sources link crude breaking and smelting to lead pollution and health harm.
Ask the seller, distributor or ARBR how to return a used battery, because the regulations place take-back responsibility on producers, importers and distributors.

categories.where_to_take: No household drop-off locations were found. Do not invent any.
gaps: Guidance for small household cells (AA, AAA, button)

facts.claim: The National Environmental (Electrical/Electronic Sector) Regulations, 2011 (S.I. No. 23 of 2011) cover new and used electrical and electronic equipment, include e-waste control, and provide for extended producer responsibility.
A 2022 version of the regulations also covers importation, EPR, e-waste handling and e-waste disposal, with buy-back provisions.
Under EPR, manufacturers, importers and distributors must take back their end-of-life products.
The E-waste Producer Responsibility Organisation Nigeria (EPRON) was established in 2018 to coordinate take-back and recycling schemes.
WHO says informal e-waste recycling, including open burning, releases lead, mercury and dioxins, and that children and pregnant women are especially vulnerable.
WHO reports informal e-waste workers can be exposed to over 1,000 harmful substances.

household_guidance.text: Do not burn electronics or take them apart informally; WHO links open burning and informal recycling to toxic exposure.
Ask the shop or brand, or EPRON, about take-back for end-of-life devices.

categories.where_to_take: No specific consumer collection points were verified. Do not invent any.
gaps: Current EPRON or producer take-back points for households
Data-wiping advice for phones and laptops

facts.claim: Lagos banned styrofoam food packs, polystyrene cups, plastic straws, plastic cutlery and nylon carrier bags under 40 microns; full enforcement began 1 July 2025 after a moratorium following the January 2024 announcement.
Enforcement targets shops and markets selling, storing or distributing the banned items, with sealing, confiscation and prosecution. The sources read do not describe penalties for households.
Styrofoam and other single-use plastics block drainage channels and canals in Lagos.
The state commissioner encouraged reusable food containers instead.

household_guidance.text: Do not throw foam packs into drains or canals.

categories.where_to_take: No recycling route for foam packs was found.
gaps: How households should dispose of foam packs (general bin via PSP is likely but unsourced)

facts.claim: Households in Lagos must keep waste bins and subscribe to licensed PSP operators; LAWMA says to contact it if the operator fails to collect.
LAWMA toll-free numbers 07080601020 and 617 (for Glo users) were listed in a roughly 2022 article. They may have changed.

household_guidance.text: When unsure what an item is or where it goes, ask LAWMA or your PSP operator.

Ask two or three local scrap dealers or recyclers what they accept for cans, glass, paper and PET, and write down what they say as a primary source.
Check whether EPRON and ARBR run any household-accessible take-back points today.
Open the 2011 and 2022 e-waste regulation PDFs and the 2024 battery regulations from official sources and confirm section numbers before citing them.
Confirm that the RecyclePoints and LAWMA buy-back points still operate.
